item: A law document whose processing raises after a good fetch is stamped like a failed request (check time, error status, 24 h back-off) instead of being re-fetched every pass
refs: R294; R189; R293 delta read; PR #1548
summary: track_document stamps last_checked_at before it fetches and commits only on its own return paths, so an exception that escaped it after the fetch (a locked commit, an extractor crash) met the batch trackers' session.rollback(), which discarded the stamp: the document stayed at the head of auto_track_due's least-recently-checked order and was fetched again on every pass with no back-off (measured on main, which carries R293: 3 requests over 3 passes; with a batch of two, two such documents at the head kept a healthy one behind them from ever being fetched in 3 passes). Now _back_off_after_crash, called by track_watched and auto_track_due after the rollback, stamps the document as a failed request is stamped (last_checked_at = now, last_status = 'error: ...' through record_text, committed), best effort: a failing database or a deleted row is logged and the pass goes on. It stamps only when BOTH hold. (1) The fetch returned a result for that document: track_document records (document id, the attempt's own time) on session.info once the fetch has returned, so a deferral, a kill-switch refusal, a one-off error reading the document and a failed commit of a deferral or refusal (no request made) stay unstamped (R293's rule); the id keeps one document's marker from vouching for another's, and track_document clears any earlier marker first, so one attempt's marker cannot vouch for a later attempt of the same document (a real failed request commits a new time and leaves the marker alone: a good fetch, a 503, then a deferral whose commit fails stays unstamped). (2) No check at or after the attempt's start is committed: a crash after its own commit (the corpus indexing, the lane row) keeps the outcome it recorded ('baseline captured', 'baseline already recorded', 'changed ...') instead of being overwritten with an error, and so does a newer check another session committed meanwhile (found by the independent reads; the committed last_checked_at is compared with >= the attempt's start). A crash makes a request, so it spends the batch: with two crashers ahead of a healthy document a batch of two reaches the healthy one on the next pass and a batch of three on the same pass (both pinned). track_watched now takes the document's id from the instance state, not from an attribute read, because after any commit the documents are expired and a one-off failure of that reload would have escaped the loop and failed the pass (POST /api/law/track would have answered 500). 20 test items in tests/test_law_crash_backoff.py; 18 mutants caught (helper not called in track_watched, not called in auto_track_due, no commit, no time stamp, no marker check, id not compared, marker never set, marker not cleared at the top of track_document, a failing back-off that raises into the pass, back-off before the rollback in each tracker, time check removed, time compared with ==, with > and with <=, time compared without the stored form, the duplicate-baseline path not re-stamping, id read as an attribute). Stated: a crash whose stamp cannot be written is retried next pass as before; a transient crash waits 24 h like a transient request failure; the time comparison assumes the stored time keeps the attempt's microseconds, which the SQLite and SQLCipher DateTime columns do; the 'version already recorded' path's re-stamp (older code) has no test of its own.
